Insofar as my assignment is to comment on the discussions rather than to give my thoughts about the case material directly, I shall attempt to illustrate ways in which the varying models used by the panelists influence their perceptions. I shall do this by focusing on salient aspects of the case that each has commented upon so as to highlight differences, as well as communalities, among them.

First, we cannot help observing that each panelist found in the patient important diagnostic features best explained by his particular frame of reference. In his opening remarks, Brenner says that he and Silverman think alike about the patient, viewing her diagnostically as a sexually inhibited, masochistic character disorder, unconsciously and conflictually attached to her father in an oedipal relationship repeated in the transference. The patient's relationship to her mother, too, is conceptualized principally on an oedipal level; for example, Miss K. sees her mother as not having wished her to grow up and become a woman, that is, develop breasts. Brenner does leave room for the earlier-than-oedipal calamities of childhood in his speculation, for example, that she wishes to take her brother's place as her parents' favorite, and in his comments concerning her wish for her mother's love.

The Legacy from Childhood: Considerations for Treatment of the Adult with Learning Disabilities

Ester Buchholz PHD

Ester Buchholz

One University Place
New York, NY 10003

Ester Buchholz  

Now and again psychoanalytic writers (Lichtenberg, 1983; Kafka, 1984) raise questions concerning treatment of adult patients with a history of learning disabilities. To date, there are few systematic presentations of the ramifications of early cognitive difficulties on later emotional functioning.

My work with adult patients with a history of learning problems suggests a demonstrable link between irregularities in perceptual and cognitive development and later psychopathology. The motivation behind this paper is to begin to clarify how this link is recognizable in psychoanalytic practice. The impact of cognitive functioning on object constancy and on the attainment of satisfying object relations is stressed. A framework for recognizing the manifestations of faulty object relations stemming from cognitive dysfunction is also proposed.

The connection between emotional development and cognitive impairment has historical antecedents. Hartmann (1952) and Weil (1953) stated that the behavior of persons who are neurologically impaired cannot be understood within the context of one system alone, but should be examined from a holistic view.

Ester Buchholz is Director, School Psychology Program, New York University; Supervisor, Child Therapy Training Program, Postgraduate Center for Mental Health; Director, Masters Program in the Psychology of Parenthood, New York University.

Prologue

Linda Gunsberg Issue Editor

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

This is a very exciting time in the history of psychoanalysis. Significant attention has been turned to fleshing out psychoanalytic theory as a developmental psychology. The first three years of life are the focus of study by developmental researchers, psychoanalytic researchers, and psychoanalysts. All are searching for more understanding of the presymbolic and early symbolic years, using different methodologies, asking different questions, and organizing their results in different ways.

Developmental researchers have asked questions regarding the competencies of infants, using tests and laboratory settings for their studies. They have found that infants are capable of many more skills and functions than previously thought. They are beginning to consider the infant-mother interaction and the infant-father interaction. Psychoanalytic researchers have studied infants in their homes and in laboratory settings, usually within the context of the infant-mother relationship. The questions they ask have to do with what can be learned about the presymbolic era, when the infant has experiences which are not represented symbolically and which are not, therefore, likely to be available to the patient and analyst. If early experiences either are not coded or are coded in a form different from that of adult memory, perhaps research and longitudinal observation can help provide the pictures, images, or “model scenes” (Lichtenberg, this volume) that are either reorganized on a symbolic level, or are lost forever.

I am reminded of a beautiful children's story by Taro Yashima, “Umbrella” (1961, pp. 30, 32). In the story, Momo gets an umbrella and a pair of boots for her third birthday. On the first rainy day, she excitedly puts on her boots, takes her umbrella, and walks “straight, like a grown-up lady!

The Transference Neurosis From the Viewpoint of Self Psychology

Jule Miller MD

Jule Miller

4524 Forest Park Boulevard
St. Louis, MO 63108

Jule Miller  

In the analysis of the self, kohut published perhaps the most extensive discussion of transference, and phenomena comparable to the transference neurosis, in the modern psychoanalytic literature. He wrote: “this monograph in its entirety deals with the specific transferences (or transferencelike structures) which are mobilized during the analysis of narcissistic personality disturbances …” (1971, p. 23). I believe that self psychology enlarges and enriches the concept of transference neurosis, and reaffirms its importance to psychoanalysis.

Before expanding on this thesis, I wish to review briefly Freud's development of the concept. It is remarkable that in the entire corpus of his work Freud uses the term “transference neurosis” only four times, first in “Remembering, Repeating, and Working Through” (1914, p. 154), twice in, “Beyond the Pleasure Principle” (1920), and for the final time in “The Question of Lay Analysis” (1926, p. 227). Freud does, however, use a number of synonyms for the term, especially in his Introductory Lectures (1916-1917), and in “Remembering, Repeating, and Working Through.” These include such terms as “transference illness,” “transformed neurosis,” artificial illness,” and “artificial neurosis.” In addition to using these synonyms Freud employs the term “new edition” in several places to refer to a description of the transference neurosis.

Jule P. Miller, Jr. is Director, St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute, and Training and Supervising Analyst, St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute.

Career Choice: The Dynamics of Self-Expression

Martin Fine MD and Ernest Wolf MD

Ernest Wolf

Suite 1010
180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, IL 60601

Ernest Wolf  

Some people need to know even during their latency years what they want to do in life. Others make their vocational decisions in later decades. Most choices of a career, however, are made during the later part of adolescence or in young adulthood. The psychodynamic factors going into these choices have rarely been studied systematically, although the psychotherapeutic or psychoanalytic treatment of young adults would seem to present an ideal group of subjects for such an investigation. One may speculate whether the scarcity of such studies is owing to the observation often made that little relevant material seems to emerge during psychoanalytic treatments or dynamic psychotherapies or whether this phenomenon represents an artifact introduced by the selective nonattention of therapists. Or perhaps, these apparent omissions express our common preoccupation with pathology together with a concomitant neglect of the dynamic factors that codetermine the more or less nonpathological behaviors such as choices of career or mate. It seemed to us useful, therefore, to bring together some material from various sources in an attempt to throw more light on the dynamic factors in these decision-making processes.

Martin Fine is an Advanced Candidate, The Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; and Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, The University of Chicago Medical School.

Ernest S. Wolf is Training and Supervising Analyst, The Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; and Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, Northwestern University Medical School.

On Transference Neurosis — The Structure and the Process: A Clinical Study

Nikolaas Treurniet MD

Nikolaas Treurniet

24, Eemnesserweg
1261HG Blaricum
The Netherlands

Nikolaas Treurniet  

Introduction

There is a difference between psychological structures and events. A structure is a state, an event is an activity, a process. Rosenblatt and Thickstun (1977), in this context, view structure as a “freeze frame” of a process in a system; as an organized product of a process that has reached a “stable steady state.” As soon as we try to catch a concept by isolating it, we risk treating a process as a state. During the last decade, psychoanalytic thinking has moved away from structures toward processes with an emphasis on development. Transference and neurosis are both concepts having a more general and static connotation than the concept of transference neurosis. A transference neurosis is not — it happens. Keeping in mind that transference and neurosis are universal, but transference neurosis is a development unique to psychoanalysis, I shall first approach its interface with the concept of neurosis and then with the side of transference. The intimate relationship between transference neurosis and psychoanalytic process will be illustrated by a clinical case.

Dr. Treurniet is a member of the Dutch Psychoanalytic Society; he is Supervising and Training Analyst at the Dutch Psychoanalytic Institute.

The direct observation of children has the disadvantage of working upon data which are easily misunderstandable; psycho-analysis is made difficult by the fact that it can only reach its data, as well as its conclusions, after long détours. But by co-operation the two methods can attain a satisfactory degree of certainty in their findings.

— Freud, 1905, p. 201

There is a wonderful passage in Mrs. Dalloway in which Woolf (1925) describes the heroine's coming to terms with her perception of a spinster-antagonist who in moments is transformed from a powerful, taciturn, prehistoric monster into “merely Miss Kilman, in a MacKintosh…. At this dwindling of the monster, Clarissa laughed” (p. 190). In this paper I explore some characteristics of a transitory phobic phenomenon typical of early childhood. These phenomena seemingly come out of nowhere and, like Clarissa's monster, just as inexplicably seem to dwindle away.

Freud (1926) attempted to address the problem of these earliest phobias in “Inhibitions, Symptoms, and Anxiety.” He was reluctant to trace them back to birth anxiety.

Melvin Singer MD

Melvin Singer

111 North 49th Street
Philadelphia, PA 19139

Melvin Singer  

Disturbances in self feelings comprise a significant portion of patients' complaints that extend the entire range of psychopathology. They reach special prominence, of course, in borderline patients where these experiences become the central focus of the early and middle stages of clinical work and their resolution the linchpin to a successful outcome. Because of their centrality, striving to understand and treat these disturbances in the subjective experience of the self has been instrumental in providing the impetus for the creation of new theoretical models. Still, with all this ferment, the possible existence of their deeper dynamic meaning as well as their metapsychological structure are not at all clear and remain a point of controversy.

Such symptomaticlike complaints as not feeling human, real, or alive, associated with profoundly distressing bodily experiences of emptiness or an inner void, as well as a sense of personality devoid of substance and a life filled with chaos and meaninglessness are included among the conscious experiences that are in large measure reflective of severe disturbances of the self organization.

Melvin Singer is Director of Residency Education in Psychiatry, Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital; Faculty, Philadelphia Association for Psychoanalysis; and Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry, University of Pennsylvania, Department of Psychiatry.

Epilogue

Philip Escoll Issue Editor

Philip Escoll

Philip Escoll  

In this issue, the contributors generally agree that an appreciation of young adulthood as a developmental phase with special tasks and vicissitudes is vital to psychoanalytic understanding and treating this group. Psychoanalysis is a valid choice for many young adults because of the depth and duration of the difficulties involved. In addition, young adults have the relative personality stability and flexibility to be responsive to analysis. The contributors also stress the importance of understanding the individual in the context of his family, and of the inclusion of sicker patients, the borderlines, within the scope of analytic inquiry and treatment. Left incompletely answered is the question of defect or defensive regression to account for the more primitive patient's pathology. Further uncertainty exists about the significance for the transference in the analysis of the young adult of the relationship with the analyst as a new object.

The contributors approach the young adult from the standpoint of structural theory, self psychology, interpersonal, object relations, and family theory. The evidence would indicate that for each author one or more of these approaches is useful and clinically relevant. Is diversity to be accepted as the prevailing approach to the young adult, or can a way be found to determine if one is more useful? Or, at a particular time in treatment or with a particular case or situation, does one prove more efficacious?

The essays in this issue demonstrate that we are beginning to understand a great deal about young adults. The many unanswered questions suggest that the essential mystery of youth in transition remains.

On the Wish to Leave with Love

Phyllis Sloate PHD

Phyllis Sloate

3 Brittany Lane
Larchmont, NY 10538

Phyllis Sloate  

This paper concerns the reevocation of unresolved conflicts related to the rapprochement subphase of the separation-individuation process during the psychotherapy of two adult women. Their earlier difficulties were reactivated with unusual intensity following important alterations in their children's developmental status, and were coalesced within the treatment setting as a conscious wish to be more autonomous from their own mothers, yet retain their mother's love. This wish represents the unconscious revival of the internal struggle to separate from a mother experienced as overly controlling, omnipotent, and intrusive. The partial resolution of associated conflicts had significant consequences for the mothering capacities of these women. The interplay between the unresolved rapprochement themes that arose and the resurgence of related anal developmental issues will be discussed. For a full description of rapprochement and its vicissitudes for the mother and the child, the reader is referred to Mahler's theory of separation-individuation (Mahler et al., 1975).

The following clinical vignettes illustrate the manner in which early failures in the object relations with their own mothers had impinged on the identification process (Benedek, 1959), influencing and interfering with these women's functioning in a specific area of mothering: the fostering of autonomy and initiative in their children.

Phyllis L. Sloate is Faculty and Supervising Psychologist, Department of Child Psychiatry, St. Luke's Hospital, New York City.

In the course of systematic longitudinal developmental studies and clinical assessments, I have paid special attention to the observable behavioral regulation of affect states for the better understanding of ego development in infants (i.e., children under 3 years of age). Some of the methods and conceptualizations developed in this process, as well as some of their clinical applications, are the subject of this paper.

The Definition, Development and Regulation of Affects, and the Concept of the Affective System

Unfortunately, the terms “affect” and “emotion” are often used interchangeably, with a confusing multitude of definitions applied to both. Basch (1976) suggested that the term emotion should be used to refer to a degree of psychological development where the level of self-object differentiation has started to allow at least some reflection on one's own subjective experiences.

History and Summary of Analysis to Date

The description of K.'s history as she presented it seems so negative: inhibitions, masochism, unhappy and restricted “throughout” childhood and adolescence, clinging to parents and brother, “always” feeling underappreciated, etc. that I found myself in response getting depressed about what I could do for her. I also wondered about the adequacy of her ego development in light of her claims that she has functioned so maladaptively and unsuccessfully, a thought I would view as in part a more or less objective clinical assessment but also as an example in the character transference of the kind of hopelessness this woman generates in others with her negative presentation. The choice of words Silverman used — “litany of complaints” — has a pejorative ring and spoke as well for the anger this woman generates in others; I had little difficulty empathizing with his feelings. Was she in fact ejected by her first therapist? Is this to be the transference-countertransference paradigm? Her insistence that life is unfair, in all ways, is an opening gambit; this is the history she elected to recount; it is an editorial, not a news story. Her history — as is true of all histories — is a symptom of her condition.

J. Alexis Burland is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry and Human Behavior, Jefferson Medical College of Thomas Jefferson University; Training and Supervising Analyst, Adult and Child/Adolescent Curricula, Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute.

Albert Mason BS

Albert Mason

Suite 305
450 N. Bedford Drive
Beverly Hills, CA 90210

Albert Mason  

It is impossible to criticize Dr. Silverman's work unless, like him, we have an overall picture of the patient, including her history, development, and the past sessions; just as it is impossible to assess the financial status of an individual by looking at one week's bank statements.

However, we are asked to tell what we would say to this patient after being privy to one week's sessions, and that can have its own validity, for it is true that at times one needs only a single malignant cell in a section or one tubercle bacillus in a specimen of sputum to make a diagnosis. Likewise, one check to a massage parlor or one contribution to the Ku Klux Klan would alert us to a character trait. Our past experience and memory of the patient is invaluable; however, the repetition compulsion which causes the patient to repeat memories and experiences is also present in ourselves and can keep us firmly attached to what we remember, believe, and understand about the patient already, and we may be compelled to repeat that which we already know. Thus, we must approach each session anew and have the courage to forget the previous sessions and our knowledge and even our conscious wish to understand the patient so that each day may show us a different patient from the one we already know. If we tie that with what we learn later then we may get something like an overall picture.

Albert Mason is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University Southern California School of Medicine, Los Angeles; Training Analyst, Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, Los Angeles.

Carol Munschauer PHD

Carol Munschauer

605 Le Brun Road

Carol Munschauer  

By definition, the treatment of so-called primitive personalities is fraught with turmoil, turbulence, and provocation. Efforts to understand the negativity and volatility of these difficult patients have inspired a growing interest in treatment technique. My purpose in this paper is to focus on the understanding and treatment of rage in the psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a young adult. In the case presented, the treatment was characterized by stony silences, oppositionalism, and persistent rage reactions on the part of the patient. Throughout the four years of the twice-a-week therapy, both the patient and myself were aware of the arduous, wearing, exasperating, seemingly futile and negativistic atmosphere of the treatment.

My initial approach was to attempt to reach the patient through the use of the internal empathic stance of Kohut (1977): that is, the careful pursuit of the patient's internal subjective experience. Since most of the time this approach was met with rage, I was led to try to use the more interpretive approach of Kernberg (1975).

Carol Ann Munschauer is Clinical Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, State University of New York at Buffalo School of Medicine; Graduate Psychotherapist, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; Candidate, Toronto Institute of Psychoanalysis.

The Canadian Psychoanalytic Society has awarded the 1986 Douglas Levin Essay Prize to Dr. Munschauer for this paper.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Tribute to Margaret S. Mahler

Anni Bergman PHD

Anni Bergman

Anni Bergman  

This volume is dedicated to the memory of Margaret S. Mahler, whose work has inspired many of the contributors. Dr. Mahler belonged to a group of pioneers in psychoanalysis who believed that naturalistic observation outside the psychoanalytic situation could yield important knowledge for psychoanalysts. She began her observational research of normal mother-child pairs in 1959, long before such research had become popular.

The early years were filled with excitement: excitement of ideas and excitement of people coming together to think and search, to observe, and to hear Dr. Mahler's incisive understanding and conceptualizing of what they observed. It is hard to remember that at the beginning all we had was Dr. Mahler's hypothesis that normal children all go through a process of psychological birth — the separation-individuation process — and her belief that this intrapsychic process could be inferred from observing mothers and their infants and toddlers in a naturalistic setting. The methodology as well as the conceptualizations evolved during the first three years of research. All of us working with Dr. Mahler had an opportunity to be part of a creative process.

What were Margaret Mahler's special qualities that could lead, in such relatively short time, to the formulations of the basic theory? She combined impeccable attention to all details with the intuition and skill of the psychoanalyst who could look to the heart of things. She never allowed the essential points to become lost in the mass of detailed observations. Nothing was too small or “unimportant” to escape her attention. She was indefatigable and would persevere at any effort until she was satisfied. She had strong opinions about what she saw, but she never clung to her opinions if new observations seemed to disprove them.

Arnold Goldberg  

It is an interesting exercise in the accumulation of the supposed raw data of analysis to see if there can be any sort of truly free association by a patient. This particular case is admittedly conducted according to one particular clinical model or theory, and the merging material should necessarily reflect that. The analyst and patient are engaged in a dialogue, and every exchange of any sort serves to redirect or reset the process. But no matter how focused the intent of the analyst was or how constrained the material may seem to be, it is the mark of any worthwhile alternative theory that it is able to perceive material that not only is congenial to its own tenets but likewise serves to expand one's vision and so to offer a more comprehensive explanation.

Psychoanalytic self psychology studies this analytic material with an aim of enabling one to fairly readily follow the dialectic between this unhappy patient and her frustrated analyst with what we hope will thereby be an added tool of understanding. It is of course easy to say that this is a mismanaged or poorly conducted analysis that should have been better done in one manner or another. It is also easy to say that everything is going along just fine and there is, indeed, light at the end of the tunnel.

Dr. Goldberg is Professor, Rush Medical School; Training and Supervising Analyst, Institute for Psychoanalysis, Chicago.

Preoedipal Roots of Perversion

Herman Roiphe MD and Eleanor Galenson MD

Eleanor Galenson

329 West 108th Street
New York, NY 10025

Eleanor Galenson  

Sexual perversions, the florid and frequently bizarre distortions of sexual identity, have attracted the attention of psychoanalytic investigators for the better part of this century. The ritualized denial of imagined castration is the central core of all perversions, and this denial is acted out through the regressive revival of the fantasy of the maternal phallus (Freud, 1905, 1927, 1938; Bak, 1968). The psychoanalytic study of the perversions, particularly that of fetishism, has increasingly implicated preoedipal factors in the constitution of the perversions.

In a series of papers on fetishism, Greenacre (1953, 1955, 1960) emphasized a specific combination of genetic influences. She pointed to disturbances in the first 18 months of life which produced an instability in the formation of the body image and which led to uncertainty of outline and fluctuation in the subjective sense of size.

Herman Roiphe is Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Mt. Sinai School of Medicine; Member of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute.

Scientific and Polemical Aspects of the Term Transference Neurosis in Psychoanalysis

Gail Reed PHD

Gail Reed

1199 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10128

Gail Reed  

Freud used the term transference neurosis in two ways. One, usually plural, is nosological and designates hysteria, phobia, and obsessional neurosis (Freud, 1917). The other, usually singular, pertains to a particular and organized development of the transference in the process of psychoanalysis. While a general term, this second meaning designates an extended clinical phenomenon unique in form to each individual analysis. It differs in this property from a term such as isolation because isolation describes a recurring formal constellation recognizable in varying situations. By formal, I refer to properties recognizable without specific ideational content.

A standard theoretical definition of the transference neurosis exists (Weinshel, 1971): the transference neurosis constitutes a recapitulation by the patient within the analytic situation of the infantile neurosis, although this definition itself is the subject of discussion about how much is reproduced and how much is a “new edition” of the infantile neurosis. However, clinical definitions of the transference neurosis which aspire to generalization are characterized by a high degree of elusiveness.

Gail S. Reed is a member of the Faculty, National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis.

Transference Neurosis, Archaic Transference, and the Compulsion to Repeat

John Gedo MD

John Gedo

Suite 3724
400 East Randolph Street
Chicago, Illinois 60601

John Gedo  

Although psychoanalysis has continued to make use of the phenomenologically based nosology of clinical psychiatry throughout its existence, it has simultaneously cast doubt on the validity of diagnostic entities rooted in the description of behavior. The most cogent explanation of the grounds for this skepticism is the widespread conviction that only the nature of the psychoanalytic process in any given case can reveal the actualities of psychopathology. The same point is sometimes stated in terms of maladaptation defined as the specific response of the individual to the more or less standard, quasi-experimental, setting of the “psychoanalytic situation.” In other words, the psychoanalytic diagnosis consists of the identification of a sequence of transference responses, wherein a wide spectrum of behavioral phenomena, both symptomatic and characterological, that were typical for a prospective analysand before the start of treatment are transformed into analyst-patient vicissitudes in the analytic setting.1

Dr. Gedo is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

1My use of the concept of “transference” in the foregoing statement is much looser than was Freud's original usage (1900, pp. 594-596), that of the “transfer” of the intensity of unconscious mentation to some preconscious thought; it conforms to his later usage (1905, p. 116), that of transference as the “new edition” of childhood impulses and fantasies, made conscious during psychoanalysis.551

Evaluating Young Adults for Analysis

Sander Abend MD

Sander Abend

1040 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10028

Sander Abend  

At the first meeting of the Discussion Group on Problems in the Psychoanalytic Treatment of Young Adults in May 1981, some questions were posed about assessing young adults in respect to their suitability for analysis, about communicating the recommendation when analysis seemed indicated, and about commencing the analytic undertaking. Emphasis was placed on attempting to identify the special features relevant to those tasks which stem from the age, developmental stage, and life situations of young adults, as distinguished from considerations that are a function of the specific character structure and psychopathology of an individual patient. A number of participants both at that and at subsequent meetings contributed accounts of their clinical experiences and the conclusions they drew from them. What follows, therefore, represents not my own ideas alone, but rather a compilation of clinical impressions gathered from a group of psychoanalytic practitioners who have had considerable experience in analyzing young adults.

We agreed not to attempt to reclarify the general criteria of analzyability taken account of in discussions of assessment.

Sander Abend is Training and Supervising Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Institute; and Editor-in-Chief, Psychoanalytic Quarterly.

Psychoanalytic views of feminine development have undergone significant changes in the course of the last 20 years. These have come about in part as a result of our growing knowledge of development in the first two years of life. Knowledge has been gained from both psychoanalytic observational research of mother-infant and, increasingly, father-infant, interactions, as well as from the analysis of patients with disturbances in early object relations. This paper is based on clinical work in these two areas and attempts to focus on early processes of internalization and identification that shape the emerging identity themes. Edgar Levenson  

I am very pleased to be participating in this ecumenical effort to correlate different models of psychoanalysis with their clinical applications. As a first caveat, it should be understood that I do not intend my remarks as a direct commentary on Dr. Silverman's obviously accomplished presentation, since an adumbrated clinical report cannot fairly be held to be an accurate representation of the work, which is a far more organic, multidimensional process. Moreover, much that is effective in any therapy operates at the margins of awareness of the therapist and is not reportable. Some of therapy even takes place outside the office, in interaction with the inevitable ubiquitous surrogate therapists: mates, parents, and friends — critics and supporters, both, of the therapeutic work. Consequently, third-party observation of a psychoanalysis is always on a different level of abstraction from the therapy under examination. It does not address a particular patient as much as a class of interactions of which the patient is an example (Bateson, 1979; Levenson, 1982).

My second caveat is in regard to the myth of a monolithic Interpersonal Psychoanalysis. There is a wide spectrum of psychoanalytic attitudes subsumed under the “interpersonal” rubric, and, as Gill (1983) has pointed out they are not necessarily highly congruent in their clinical approaches.

Charles Brenner  

In my opening remarks I shall try to illustrate not only how I think about this or any other patient, but also why I think as I do.

My main point is this: conflict and compromise formation are of central importance in psychic functioning. All psychic activity, including neurotic symptoms and character traits, is a compromise among drive derivatives, anxiety and depressive affect, defense and superego. In this patient, staying away from men, hating them, clinging to her parents and to her analyst, her masturbation fantasy about the mad scientist and his nurse — all are so determined. One cannot ask, therefore, “Is this defense? Has this to do with castration or with loss of love? Is this gratifying? Is this self-punitive?” The answer will always be “Yes” to each such question. What one wants to know is the answer to the question, “Which determinant of this compromise formation is it most useful to interpret to this patient at this time?” To answer it for any patient at any time one must know much more than what that patient said in this or that analytic hour. One must have an overall understanding of the patient's dynamics. One must understand what that patient's most important conflicts are, and one must follow a line of interpretation which is based on that understanding.

Epilogue: Transference Neurosis: A Phenomenon in Search of a Referent

Allan Rosenblatt Issue Co-Editor

Allan Rosenblatt

Allan Rosenblatt  

The heart of psychoanalysis is, by general agreement, the theoretical notion of unconscious motivation. Its guts are believed by many to be the clinical encounter with the transference neurosis. To question this phenomenon or tamper with it is considered, then, to be tantamount to evisceration of clinical theory and practice.

Yet in this issue Reed had deftly chronicled the varieties of surplus meaning and ideological baggage that the term has come to acquire since its original use by Freud to describe a phenomenon he encountered in his early clinical practice. She rightly urges us to divest the term of polemics and to focus more clearly on its clinical grounds. Nonetheless, despite its ambiguities, tautologies, and inconsistencies, Treurniet and Jacobs view the term as usefully encompassing clinical phenomena that they sensitively delineate in case vignettes. London forthrightly defends the use of the term and offers a process definition of the concept in reference to the formal characteristics of play. Cooper, on the other hand, argues persuasively that the term is obsolete, referring to a phenomenon that is inconsistently present and can be considered merely a quantitative variation of omnipresent transference manifestations.

Discussion: In Defense of the Transference Neurosis Concept: A Process and Interactional Definition

Nathaniel London MD

Nathaniel London

1837 Medical Arts Bldg.
Minneapolis, MN 55402

Nathaniel London  

The transference neurosis concept is subject to varying definitions and usages. Yet the term is well established in clinical theory and involves developments within the psychoanalytic situation of profound importance. My defense of the term, which includes its redefinition, is based on the following questions:

1. To what degree is a transference neurosis recognized by the nature of the clinical process at a particular point in the course of an analysis and to what degree is it recognized by particular contents, such as oedipal conflicts?

2. Is transference neurosis distinguishable from the general category of transference? The relation of these terms to the infantile neuorsis, the adult neurosis, and to core oedial conflicts is pertinent to the discussion.

3. Can a transference neurosis be specified by clinical data or is it better viewed as a theoretical concept—an operational guide to organize certain conceptions of the clinical data?

The Analyst as Participant

Merton Gill MD

Merton Gill

912 South Wood Street
Box 6998
Chicago, IL 60680

Merton Gill  

Rather than attempt a comprehensive critique of the rich data and commentaries, I propose to organize my remarks on the single issue of the analyst as a participant in an interaction. I do so because that is a special interest of mine, because I believe it is the principal key to understanding what has gone wrong with this therapy, and because it is either neglected or referred to only allusively by most of the discussants.

My thesis can be simply stated: the primary manifest theme in the patient's content is one that she experiences as also being enacted with the analyst. The patient portrays herself as misunderstood, unappreciated, and imposed upon by others, and she experiences the analyst as misunderstanding, failing to appreciate her, and imposing himself upon her. This theme manifests itself between them in many ways, ranging from his imposing his ideas on her to his assaulting her sexually in a sadomasochistic relationship — metaphorically of course.

It is particularly interesting that the analyst explicitly considers the possibility of his being drawn into a sadomasochistic interaction and warns himself to guard against it. But what he considers to be the danger is what I believe is in fact taking place, namely that he is involved in such an interaction.

Merton M. Gill is Professor of Psychiatry, University of Illinois Medical School, Chicago; Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute of Psychoanalysis.

Notes on The Unknowable; Analytic Secrets and The Transference Neurosis

Theodore Jacobs MD

Theodore Jacobs

170 E. 77 Street
New York, NY 10021

Theodore Jacobs  

Although generally regarded as the quintessential element in the analytic process and among its most distinguishing features, the phenomenon known as the transference neurosis remains an area whose full dimensions have yet to be explored.

In this paper I discuss certain covert interactions between patient and analyst that, communicated in subtle and often unconscious ways, may constitute essential, if often overlooked, aspects of the transference neurosis.

The importance of secrets in family life and in child development is well known and has been the subject of recent papers by Caruth (1985), Michaels (1985), and Rusten (1985). In a previous publication (1980) I discussed their role in the analytic situation and noted that it is not rare in analysis for secretive collusions to exist between patient and therapist. In this communication I take up another aspect of secrets and illustrate how they may enter into the formation of the transference neurosis. In doing so I discuss secrets kept not only by the patient but also by the analyst and how the interplay of the mutual need for secrecy may affect the development, uncovering, and working through of aspects of the transference neurosis.

Dr. Jacobs is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Albert Einstein College of Medicine; he is on the Faculties of The New York Psychoanalytic Institute and The Psychoanalytic Institute at New York University.

Having had access only to Dr. Silverman's written text prevents me from hearing between the lines as one tends to do when a colleague presents clinical material — such as the tone of voice in which he made his interpretations. Did he sound cross? Amused? Sympathetic? Also there are many vitally important questions that remain unanswered. For example, about Miss K.'s early childhood. Was she ever ill? What were her earliest memories? What had she heard about her parents' desire for this second child? Was she a “change-of-life” baby or did she arrive right on the heels of the first child? Had she been led to believe that her parents would have preferred another son? How much older was her brother? Old enough to be a parent-substitute, or young enough to be an intensely invested rival? What about her mother's pregnancy and her fantasies about the child she was expecting? Then the birth itself and the parents' reactions?

These questions hammer at my mind because it is difficult to see why K. considers herself so undesired, unloved, uncared for, and unappreciated. The fact of her being a girl offers little explanation. She of course interpreted her parents' negative attitudes in this way as a certain number of women patients do. But it's an easy alibi. K.'s recollection of the early family history provides me with very few clues as to the possible causes of her intense bitterness and sadness.

Miss K., 25 years old, was referred for analysis by a psychiatrist with whom she had been in psychotherapy in college in another location. She showed sexual and social inhibitions, masochistic tendencies, and chronic, neurotic depression. The details which she presented amounted to a litany of complaints and grudges over injuries and slights she could neither forget nor forgive. Epilogue

Sydney Pulver Issue Editor

Sydney Pulver

Sydney Pulver  

One ineluctable conclusionemerges clearly from this study: an analyst's theoretical orientation has a marked impact on the way he thinks about patients and the way he works with them. This conclusion raises an equally striking question: how can clinicians who think and behave so differently get equally good analytic results? Before addressing these points let me consider some of the problems inherent in the use of the methodology from which they have arisen.

The private nature of psychoanalytic data has always been the subject of scientific frustration and criticism, most recently by Grünbaum (1984). Spence (1986) clearly demonstrated the inadequacy of most psychoanalytic reports for explanatory purposes, as contrasted with their interpretive use, and made an eloquent plea for the development of more adequate approaches to psychoanalytic reporting. Audio- and videorecording, while a step in the right direction, runs aground on the volume of data that must be explored, a volume unmanageable for many purposes.

The method of data collection used in this study, a brief case presentation followed by process notes taken by the treating analyst at the time of the session, is the backbone of psychoanalytic supervision and has been used since the dawn of psychoanalytic history. It is, of course, essentially different from data obtained via supervision in that the material being studied is presented in written form rather than in person verbally by the analyst. This has the virtue of making the data more publicly available, but at the price of omitting much of the nonverbal affective contents of the analyst's report and rendering impossible closer investigation through questioning about specific aspects of the analytic exchange. Like all methods of presenting psychoanalytic material, this one has its problems.

Prologue

Sydney Pulver Issue Editor

Sydney Pulver

Sydney Pulver  

This issue of psychoanalytic inquiry takes off from a panel I chaired at the Annual Meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association in Denver, in May, 1985. The title of the panel, The Relationship of Models of the Mind to Clinical Work, was fairly explicit in stating its purpose. In an attempt to explore the relation between theory and clinical work, detailed clinical material gathered by an analyst of one theoretical persuasion would be the focus of discussion by analysts of other theoretical persuasions. In this case the presenter is an adherent of structural theory.

The format for the panel was simple. A respected clinician, one clearly an adherent of structural theory, would present a short summary of a patient's history, the course of the analysis up to the present, and process notes on several consecutive sessions. This material would then be submitted to four discussants of different theoretical stances, who would offer their views of the patient's dynamics and their own therapeutic approach. We emphasized that we wanted a personal discussion rather than one representative of the theory espoused.

The task of enlisting a colleague to provide the clinical material was not as difficult as I had anticipated. I was, after all, asking someone to put his clinical practice on the line in a way that is rather unusual in psychoanalysis (except for candidates!), and I expected to meet with a certain amount of reluctance. Happily, the first person I called, Dr. Martin Silverman, agreed to participate. As he stated in a letter “… I would have taken notes on the first patient I saw after speaking with you, but he was a silent, intensely resistant patient who would not have offered useful material. So I simply took notes on the next patient's sessions. I think the material will do.” As the reader will see, it does very well indeed.

Psychoanalysis of Young Adults: An Overview

Philip Escoll MD

Philip Escoll

111 North 49th Street
Philadelphia, PA 19139

Philip Escoll  

Was shaw accurate in saying, “Youth is wasted on the young?” His observation reflects envy of youth and perhaps a tendency to idealize youth and young adulthood as a carefree time of energy, sexuality, joy, freshness, and experimentation. These elements are present, but as we know from clinical analytic experience as well as from some of the studies about young adulthood, it is also a time of much travail and vulnerability. If it is true that this is a time of vulnerability, how is this explained when young adulthood is seen through all the literature as a time of psychic consolidation? Why all the recent attention to young adults and to young adulthood as a phase? Is there anything different or special about this time of life and about the analysis of young adults?

In this paper I attempt to respond to these questions.

Philip J. Escoll is Training and Supervising Analyst, Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Pennsylvania; and Senior Attending Psychiatrist, Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital.

The Family in the Psychoanalysis of the Young Adult

Roger Shapiro MD

Roger Shapiro

2312 Tracy Place, Northwest
Washington, DC 20008

Roger Shapiro  

In the years following Freud's abandonment of the seduction hypothesis, interpretations of family experience in psychoanalytic treatment tended to view the patient's internal conception of his family relationships as a subjective distortion, rather than as containing actual characteristics of the parent-child relationship. This internal conception of the family was based on a theory of a maturing drive and defensive organization in the individual that required objects in the family for drive discharge, but did not emphasize the actual characteristics of the relationships with objects. Conflicts within the individual over the build-up of instinctual needs and the internal consequences of defense and delay in drive discharge were the concepts most relied upon to explain symptoms.

During the past 40 years this emphasis has shifted. Many psychoanalytic investigators, among them Erikson (1950, 1968), Jacobson (1964), Klein (1953, 1957), Winnicott (1958, 1965), Fairbairn (1952), Mahler et al. (1975), Kohut (1971, 1977), and Loewald (1980), have focused increasing attention on the actual characteristics of parent-child relationships as important determinants of the developing child's drive and structural organization.

Roger L. Shapiro is a member of the Faculty, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute; and Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, George Washington University School of Medicine.

Arnold Cooper MD

Arnold Cooper

525 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Arnold Cooper  

The refinement of the traditional terminology of psychoanalysis is an important task for psychoanalysts today. As I have indicated elsewhere (Cooper, 1986) out uncritical use of a language that was developed in a psychoanalytic era quite different from our own is a source of confusion in our discipline. Terms that had relatively clear meanings, referring to seemingly simple concepts in the prestructural era of psychoanalysis or in the period before the recent advances in infant research, ego psychology, and object relations theory, may no longer have clear definition in our newer frames of reference. Moreover, a significant portion of our technical language has never been clearly defined and was presented by Freud to encapsulate important ideas with the overt or tacit aim that clinical experience with the concepts among psychoanalysts would lead to clarification of meanings. The concepts of the transference neurosis and its almost essential companion idea, the infantile neurosis, are examples of this usage.

The term transference neurosis has, for many psychoanalysts, become inextricable within a definition of psychoanalysis. At a Panel (1981)

Martin Silverman  

Sydney Pulver's request that I provide material to serve as a springboard for a panel on the influence of models of the mind on clinical work seemed to afford an opportunity not only to contribute something useful to psychoanalysis but also to obtain the consultative assistance of a group of thoughtful, experienced psychoanalysts that might be helpful to me in my work. I welcomed the opportunity to present material from an ongoing analysis to four (later expanded to eight) dedicated and esteemed colleagues. I elected to present a series of hours from my work with the first patient I was to see the next day (though I had to settle for the second patient, because the first one was going through a largely silent phase in his analysis). Although my aim was to present random analytic material, I was not unaware that I would be obtaining the benefit of observations on a very difficult case, a case which I believe any psychoanalyst would find very difficult.

As I understand it and make use of it in my work, the structural model utilizes a multidimensional, multifaceted approach to human psychology that is broad enough to cover an extremely wide range of normal and pathological phenomena, yet is sufficiently specific and consistent to do so coherently and comprehensively.

An Object Relations Perspective

Arnold Modell MD

Arnold Modell

401 Woodward Street
Waban, MA 02168

Arnold Modell  

Our fundamental theoretical assumptions, our Model of the Mind, undoubtedly has a profound influence on our understanding of an analytic case. One's model of psychoanalysis has an organizing effect, it selects our responses and interpretations; our theoretical preconceptions determine how we conduct an analysis. Different models of the mind may not lead to widely divergent techniques, as we all adhere to certain basic technical methods such as avoiding overactivity, not giving reassurance, creating an ambience that will permit the full emergence of the patient's capacity to free associate, and so forth. But while we may not differ in our fundamental technique, what we select to focus upon will have an enormous influence on the unfolding of the analytic process; the raw data of analysis is multidetermined and ambiguous, offering a multiplicity of meanings, all of which may be in a certain sense true. The crucial issue, however, is the analyst's recognition of what is immediate and “real’ and what is being used for purposes of defense and dissimulation.

The model of the mind that seems to have influenced Dr. Silverman is that of classical analysis with its emphasis on the centrality of Oedipus complex. My differences with him are not such that I would propose any fundamental alteration of basic technique.

Dr. Modell is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School at the Beth Israel Hospital; Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute.

Prologue

Philip Escoll Issue Editor

Philip Escoll

Philip Escoll  

What accounts for the increasing attention psychoanalysts and other mental health professionals are focusing today on young adults? Many factors contribute to this upsurge of interest. As the moratorium needed by some adolescents before taking on adult responsibilities and career choices (Erikson, 1956) has been stretched with more time spent in college, graduate school, and postdoctoral training, society has become increasingly aware of a group identified as “young adults.” A population growth in this age span has also compelled us to be mindful of this phase. Student health units in colleges have been organized to deal with the stressful psychological demands upon students; psychiatric consultation and treatment services have expanded. Over the last five to ten years, psychiatric facilities have opened special units in mental and general hospitals devoted to treating those in the 18 to 25 period of life. Increasing numbers of chronically mentally ill young adults reside in hospitals. Many others congregate near hospitals or university centers, often unemployed or working sporadically — and frequently alcohol and substance abusers. In addition, the increase in suicide in the young adult period has been startling. Among 15-to 24-year-olds, the rate has more than doubled since 1961. The vulnerability of young people in this period is further indicated by the high incidence of narcissistic and borderline personality disorders and severe eating dysfunctions.

All these developments draw our concern and interest to the young adult. As psychoanalytic developmental theory has expanded, moving in its exploration and conceptualizations both to infants and to the adult, mid-life and older adult years, psychoanalysts increasingly regard development as a lifelong process.

Clinical Applications of a Psychoanalytic Systems Model of Assertion and Aggression

Gerald Stechler PHD

Gerald Stechler

18 Whittier Road
Lexington, MA 02173

Gerald Stechler  

Picture the following situation. We are in an infant and toddler day care center. The children come here every weekday and spend most of the day here. Some have been coming for several months, and some are newly arrived. On the floor, near the center of a well-lighted playroom, a young but experienced child-care worker is sitting with a newly enrolled eight-month-old girl, Laura. The worker is talking to the girl and showing her some blocks. About three feet away a 14-month-old girl, Jane, is also sitting on the floor looking at the other two. Jane has a push toy with a musical wheel at the end of it. She is moving it with her left hand, slowly and then more forcefully advancing it toward Laura. The worker responds by first positioning her body to protect Laura, and then by reaching out and removing the toy from Jane's hand. As she does this, she says to Jane, “Why don't you do it with your other hand?” At that point she brings the toy around and puts it in Jane's right hand. Jane has plenty of open space on her right side, and starts to push the toy in that direction with increasing vigor. Her facial expression becomes more joyfully excited. Finally she stands up and walks the toy across the room, pleasantly vocalizing.

A Developmentalist Perspective

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 Eighteenth Street, N. W.
Washington, DC 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

The developmentalist perspective as I employ it takes the traditional genetic point of view (finding causal linkages between past and present) and amplifies it through a focus on the possibilities for subjective experience and psychic organization present at each stage of development. As applied to the task of discovering the overt and hidden meanings in Dr. Silverman's clinical example, the developmentalist perspective asks a number of questions. What problematic patterns of experiencing and interacting persist, and how are these to be explained? When psychologically significant events occur in the course of treatment, are there “model scenes” from critical developmental phases that match and give conceptual coherence to these events? Assuming the analyst to be a concerned, sensitive, empathic therapist, how does his plasticity allow the analysand to induce him into a role having conscious and unconscious significance to the analysand from her prior experience?

Two problematic patterns stand out in Miss K.'s pretreatment history and in the hours recorded in the transcript: her angry, persecutory-like orientation and her uncomfortable inability to come to terms with her femininity. While these two problems are in all probability interrelated, each could exist without the other, so it is reasonable to regard their roots as possibly separate.

Dr. Lichtenberg is a practicing Psychoanalyst, Washington, DC; Faculty Member, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

The Borderline Father: Reconstructions of Young Adulthood

Melvin Lansky MD

Melvin Lansky

1100 Glendon Avenue
Suite 1527
Los Angeles, CA 90024

Melvin Lansky  

The purpose of this communication is to shed light on the impact of borderline psychopathology on the transition in young adulthood from the developmental tasks of adolescence, to the tasks, fatherhood in particular, of adulthood proper. The tasks of adolescence include separation from family of origin, consolidation of sexual identity, and the beginnings of the capacities to work and love in adult life. By the end of young adulthood, say at the age of 25 or 26, a healthy or even neurotic person should have some capacity to work and to form a satisfying, generative love relationship. The interference with these normal developmental tasks by so-called borderline pathology in a young adult affects intimate relationships, the capacity to work, the capacity for stable marital relationships, and an expanded capacity for involvement in relationships that are not tied to immediate defensive needs. These developmental attainments are sharply, and sometimes decisively, tested in the young adult man by the emergence into fatherhood. In the paternal role, the young adult must be able to provide emotional and material support for mother and child and to tolerate the loss of the exclusiveness of the dyadic relationship in the marriage.

Melvin R. Lansky is Adjunct Professor of Psychiatry, University of California, Los Angeles Medical School; Staff Psychiatrist and Chief, Family Treatment Program, Brentwood Veterans Administration Medical Center; and Faculty, Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Institute.

Epilogue

Linda Gunsberg Issue Editor

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

In general, the following points can be highlighted when attempting to dovetail findings about the early years with adult development. First, earlier forms and organizations are never fully relinquished. They may be in the periphery waiting to be activated, they can coexist with higher levels of organization, and even overlap with more complex reorganizations and structures. Most importantly, they are the fundamental units upon which higher levels of organization are built. The more seriously disturbed the patient, the more likely we will be dealing with these fundamental processes on a regular basis. These longitudinal observations offer specificity and refinements that were previously unavailable to us regarding these fundamental units. Second, infantile disturbances such as aversions and fetishes can serve adaptive functions and disappear later in life.

Third, often when we deal with the intrapsychic model of conflict, we overemphasize the wishes and fantasies of our patients and underestimate both the real, competent, and original parenting some adults have been fortunate to have had as well as the seriously deficient parenting of others. Some of these studies remind us of the severe consequences of a depressed mother, of the mother who cannot let her child be a separate person with his or her own gender, or of the effect of a mother's problems on her own affect regulation and thus her inability to regulate the child's affects early in life.

Now, let us review each contribution regarding applications to adult treatment. Lichtenberg has urged all analysts to keep in mind the complex interrelationship between early regulatory efforts/dysfunctions and intrapsychic conflicts. He has distinguished between disturbances that are a source of conflict and those which are the result of conflict.

Infant Studies and Clinical Work with Adults

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 18th Street NW
Washington, DC 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

During a workshop on the relevance of infant observational research for clinical work with adults held at the American Psychoanalytic Association Meeting in New York, November 1982, two contradictory points of view were argued. One view of the infant, presented by Charles Brenner, stated that the psychological organization of the neonate and young toddler differs so markedly and undergoes so much transformation during the oedipal period that knowledge of the infant can have no or only a very limited influence on the conduct of the analysis of an adult. A second view presented by both James McLaughlin and myself stated that recognition of the complex behavior of infants revealed by infant studies calls for a radical reconception of development. Thus, although symbolic processing is absent until the middle of the second year or even because its absence raises questions about efforts to reconstruct developmental events of the first 18 months, the knowledge that emerges from infant studies has influenced and cannot fail to continue to shape significant aspects of analytic work with adults (see Gedo, 1979, 1985; Lichtenberg, 1983a; Gaensbauer, 1985).

Dr. Lichtenberg is on the Faculty, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.
